summary: Defines a RELOAD usage for managing shared write access to resources, using a hierarchical trust delegation scheme with an access list and a new USER-CHAIN-ACL policy.

eli5.summary: A shared notebook where an owner can pass writing rights to others, who can pass them on.

questions: how does reload shared write access work
how are reload acl delegations revoked
subtitle: How RELOAD peers can share write access to one overlay location through a chain of signed delegations.

tldr.problem: In a RELOAD overlay only the holder of a certificate may write at a given location, so several peers cannot jointly maintain one shared resource.
tldr.mechanism: The resource owner stores an access control list of signed delegations next to the data, and a new USER-CHAIN-ACL policy lets storing peers accept writes from anyone with a valid chain back to the owner.
tldr.outcome: Groups can run rendezvous and coordination services on a single identifier. The owner can revoke a whole branch of delegations with one overwrite, but the ACL is publicly readable.

today: RFC 8076 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2017. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 6940.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RELOAD, defined in RFC 6940, is a peer-to-peer protocol that lets applications add behaviour through Usages. RFC 8076 defines a Usage called ShaRe (Shared Resources in RELOAD) for managing shared write access to RELOAD Resources.

Normally RELOAD lets a peer write only at a small set of well-defined locations (Resource-IDs) tied to the username or Node-ID in its certificate. ShaRe extends this so that multiple users can write to a common Resource-ID in a controlled way. The RFC names third-party registration (see RFC 7904) and distributed conferencing as target uses, especially rendezvous, where one identifier points to several dynamic instances of a cooperative service.

The document has two parts: trust delegation through an Access Control List (ACL), and an optional way to store Resources under a variable name.
sections.eli5: Usually only one person can write at one spot in the shared network. ShaRe lets that person invite others to write there too, in a controlled way.

sections.title: Owners, Authorized Peers and Shared Resources
sections.content:
The RFC defines four terms. A Shared Resource is a Resource with its Kinds that several users may write. The Resource Owner is the peer that first stored it and holds the certificate granting write access. An Authorized Peer was given write access by the owner or by another Authorized Peer. The Access Control List is a logical list of users allowed to write a given Resource/Kind pair.

Sharing takes two steps: store the Resource/Kind pairs to be shared, then store an ACL for those Kinds. Delegation can include the right to delegate further, which produces a tree of trust delegations with the owner as the trust anchor at its root.

A Kind can be shared only if it follows three rules:

  • It uses the array or dictionary data model with data isolation, so each item is maintained only by the user who created it.
  • Its Usage uses the USER-CHAIN-ACL access policy.
  • If the overlay configuration allows variable resource names, the Kind data starts with a ResourceNameExtension field.
sections.eli5: One kid owns the notebook, and friends with a pass can write in it. Each friend can only change their own pages, so nobody scribbles over anybody else.

sections.title: Isolating Data and the ACL Structure
sections.content:
To avoid race conditions, each stored item belongs to the user who wrote it. In a dictionary, the key MUST be the Node-ID of the certificate used to sign the data. In an array, each writer gets its own index range: take the least significant 24 bits of the signing Node-ID and append an 8-bit individual index. The resulting 32-bit integer MUST be the array index, so each peer can create 256 distinct entries. If a collision does happen, the Storing Peer refuses to overwrite.

The ACL itself is an array stored at the same overlay location as the Shared Resource. Each entry is an AccessControlListItem with these fields:

  • res_name_ext: optional, used for variable resource names.
  • to_user: the username that obtains write permission.
  • kind: the Kind-ID being shared.
  • allow_delegation: if true, that user may add further ACL entries for the Kind.

Every Authorized Peer signs its own ACL items, so others can check who granted what. The RFC also notes that delegation need not be loop free: circular delegations between two users are possible, though not very meaningful.
sections.eli5: Each friend gets their own numbered stack of pages, built from part of their name, so page numbers never clash. The list of who may write is signed by whoever added each name.

sections.title: Variable Resource Names
sections.content:
Some uses, such as conferencing, need names beyond the username or Node-ID in the certificate. ShaRe lets an overlay define patterns for Resource Names in the overlay configuration document. A sample pattern in the RFC is .*-conf-$USER@$DOMAIN. The name stays tied to the owner's certificate because the pattern must contain the user and domain parts.

The ResourceNameExtension structure carries a type (only pattern is defined) and the Resource Name, so any receiver can check that the name hashes to the Resource-ID. Patterns are POSIX Extended Regular Expressions, both $USER and $DOMAIN MUST appear, and the variable part MUST be separated from the username part by a fixed delimiter.

The delimiter matters. With a pattern like *$USER, user EVE could define a resource named STEVE and block the name for user STEVE. The feature is off by default: the enable attribute of variable-resource-names defaults to false.
sections.eli5: Normally your mailbox name is just your name. This lets you also use names like 'yourname-party', as long as a fixed word keeps them from clashing with someone else's name.

sections.title: Granting, Revoking and Validating Access
sections.content:
To share a Kind, the owner stores an ACL root item at the Resource-ID with its own username, the Kind-ID and allow_delegation set to 1. It then adds items for Authorized Peers, optionally setting ad to 1 (the default is 0) so they can delegate further. An Authorized Peer with ad=1 can add items in the same way. An attempt to overwrite an ACL item signed by someone else gets an Error_Forbidden response.

Revoking means storing a nonexistent value at the item. This also invalidates every delegation made by that user and all later ones, so a whole subtree is cut with one operation. Overwriting the root invalidates the entire tree. Only the user who stored an item, or the owner, may overwrite it. The owner SHOULD overwrite invalidated subtrees to protect users' privacy.

To validate a write, a peer walks the chain: find an ACL item whose to_user equals the signer's username, then repeatedly check the signer of that item has an item with ad=1, until it reaches the root item, which must be signed by the owner of the ACL Resource. The chain is valid only if every step succeeds. Validation can be skipped when the owner itself wrote the data.
sections.eli5: To check a pass, you follow the signatures back: who let this kid in, and who let that person in, until you reach the notebook's owner. Cross out one name and everyone that person invited loses their pass too.

sections.title: The USER-CHAIN-ACL Policy and Peer Duties
sections.content:
The new USER-CHAIN-ACL policy lets Authorized Peers write a Shared Resource without owning the matching certificate. A store request MUST be denied if neither USER-MATCH nor USER-NODE-MATCH from RFC 6940 applies (the latter is mandatory for dictionaries), if the signer's username does not fit a configured naming pattern, if the hashed Resource Name does not match the Resource-ID, or if the ACL check fails.

Storing peers MUST run the validation on every incoming store request using the most recent ACL, and SHALL ensure only the owner stores new ACL root items. Accessing peers can verify data by fetching the ACL: send a Stat request to the Resource-ID, then fetch the listed array indexes. They may cache ACLs up to the maximum lifetime of an item, but SHOULD use a Stat request to check for updates first.

The RFC also defines the ACCESS-CONTROL-LIST Kind: an array whose Resource Name is the name of the Kind being shared, protected by USER-CHAIN-ACL.
sections.eli5: The notebook keeper checks every new page against the signed list before accepting it. Anyone reading can do the same check.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC lists four concerns.

  • Resource exhaustion: many peers may write many entries to one resource. Setting a max-size for the Kind in the configuration document limits this.
  • Misbehaving storing peer: it could withhold data, a denial of service for the group, but it could not return forged data because signatures can be verified.
  • Bad delegation: a malicious Authorized Peer can interfere and may authorize more collaborators. The owner must delegate only to trustworthy peers and can revoke a whole tree in one overwrite.
  • Privacy: all data in a Shared Resource is readable by any node in the overlay, so private data needs encryption. The ACL must be unencrypted, so group membership is publicly visible.
sections.eli5: A bad helper can cause trouble, but the owner can cancel a whole branch of passes at once. Anyone can read the notebook and the guest list, so secrets need a lock.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered three things for ShaRe. The USER-CHAIN-ACL entry went into the RELOAD Access Control Policies registry. The ACCESS-CONTROL-LIST Kind was registered in the RELOAD Data Kind-ID registry with Kind-ID 0x4. The XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:p2p:config-base:share was registered for the configuration extension.
sections.eli5: The new rule and the new kind of list were written into the official catalogs so everyone uses the same names.
